crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Reading regulatory filings is the practice of pulling useful signals from the documents public companies and funds must file with regulators. For AI-related instruments, that means annual reports, quarterly reports, current reports, registration statements, proxy statements, and merger and acquisition filings. The work covers risk factors, management discussion and analysis, litigation disclosures, related-party transactions, and executive compensation. It also covers the footnotes, where accounting policies and segment data often reveal how an AI business actually earns money.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The basic infrastructure is a browser, a spreadsheet, and a reliable feed of filings from EDGAR or a commercial terminal. For AI-related names, a site like this one tracks 117 listed AI-related instruments with daily prices, so you can line up a filing date with the market's reaction. Document parsing tools and PDF extractors help when you need to search across hundreds of pages. Some teams add natural language processing to flag changes in risk language, but the core work still runs on careful reading.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts with a question, such as how much revenue an AI segment actually contributes or what a company says about a pending lawsuit. You pull the filing, read the relevant sections, and compare the language to the prior quarter or year. A simple checklist helps: risk factors, management discussion, footnotes, and exhibits. For deals, the merger proxy often includes a background section that explains how the transaction came together, and this site tracks 355 merger and acquisition filings for that purpose. Cross-referencing with active AI lawsuits can show whether a disclosed case is routine or material.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Filings are public records, but their provenance matters: EDGAR is the official source, while third-party databases can introduce errors or lag. The risk is not just legal, it is analytical, because a footnote can change the meaning of a headline number. Forward-looking statements are protected by safe harbor rules, but that does not make them true. This site tracks 148 active AI lawsuits, which shows how often disclosed litigation becomes a material issue. Nothing here is legal advice, and reading a filing does not give you the right to trade on non-public information.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward more machine-readable filings, with inline XBRL and structured data making it easier to pull numbers directly. Large language models are being used to summarize and compare long documents, though they still need a human to check the citations. Regulators are adding AI-specific disclosure requirements, so the volume of relevant text will keep growing. This site lists 732 AI tools, and some of them are built for document review. The professional skill will shift from finding the filing to asking the right question of it.
